theme: The vision of Christ, the risen Lord among his churches
readingInstruction: Read Revelation 1:1-20 in one sitting. This is the opening of the last book of the Bible. Notice how often the language echoes the Old Testament, and how the book begins and ends with Jesus Christ, not with a timetable of events.
settingTheScene: The apostle John, now an old man, was exiled on the island of Patmos in the Aegean Sea around AD 95, during the reign of the emperor Domitian, when emperor worship was pressing on the churches of Asia Minor. Revelation is a letter to seven real churches, a prophecy, and an apocalypse: a kind of writing that uses symbols and visions to unveil what is true behind the surface of history. It is full of images drawn from Daniel, Ezekiel, Isaiah, Zechariah, Exodus, and the Psalms, and nearly every verse echoes the Old Testament. It is not a puzzle to decode but a vision to be seen and a book to be heard. Its message to suffering believers is: Jesus reigns, and the Lamb wins.
observation: “Blessed is the one who reads aloud the words of this prophecy, and blessed are those who hear, and who keep what is written in it, for the time is near” (v. 3).
“To him who loves us and has freed us from our sins by his blood” (v. 5).
“Behold, he is coming with the clouds, and every eye will see him” (v. 7).
“I am the Alpha and the Omega, says the Lord God, who is and who was and who is to come, the Almighty” (v. 8).
“I, John, your brother and partner in the tribulation and the kingdom and the patient endurance that are in Jesus” (v. 9).
“From his mouth came a sharp two-edged sword, and his face was like the sun shining in full strength” (v. 16).
“I died, and behold I am alive forevermore, and I have the keys of Death and Hades” (v. 18).
“The seven stars are the angels of the seven churches, and the seven lampstands are the seven churches” (v. 20).
interpretation:
The book begins, “The revelation of Jesus Christ.” The Greek word is apokalypsis, an unveiling. It is a revelation from Jesus and about Jesus. And it begins with a blessing, the first of seven in the book: “Blessed is the one who reads aloud the words of this prophecy, and blessed are those who hear, and who keep what is written in it.” It was meant to be read aloud in the churches and obeyed. “The time is near” means that its message presses on every generation.

The greeting is to the seven churches in Asia, from the triune God: from him “who is and who was and who is to come” (the Father), from the “seven spirits who are before his throne” (the Holy Spirit in his fullness), and from Jesus Christ, “the faithful witness, the firstborn of the dead, and the ruler of kings on earth.” Notice the three titles: he witnessed faithfully, he rose first, and he rules even over the emperor. Then a burst of praise: “To him who loves us and has freed us from our sins by his blood and made us a kingdom, priests to his God and Father, to him be glory and dominion forever and ever. Amen.” This borrows the language of Exodus 19:6 and applies it to the church, as Peter does. Then a promise combining Daniel 7:13 and Zechariah 12:10: “Behold, he is coming with the clouds, and every eye will see him, even those who pierced him, and all tribes of the earth will wail on account of him.” And God himself speaks: “I am the Alpha and the Omega,” the first and last letters of the Greek alphabet, the beginning and the end.

John describes himself as a “brother and partner in the tribulation and the kingdom and the patient endurance that are in Jesus.” Those three are always together for Christians: suffering, kingdom, and endurance. He was on Patmos “on account of the word of God and the testimony of Jesus.” On the Lord’s day (Sunday, the day of Christ’s resurrection) he was “in the Spirit” and heard a loud voice like a trumpet telling him to write what he sees to the seven churches.

He turns and sees seven golden lampstands, and in the midst “one like a son of man” (Daniel 7:13). His description is overwhelming: a long robe and golden sash, hair white like wool, eyes like a flame of fire, feet like burnished bronze, voice like the roar of many waters, in his right hand seven stars, from his mouth a sharp two-edged sword, and his face like the sun in full strength. Almost every feature recalls the Old Testament’s descriptions of God and the Ancient of Days. Jesus is portrayed as divine, glorious, and terrifying. John falls at his feet as though dead. But Jesus lays his right hand on him and says, “Fear not, I am the first and the last, and the living one. I died, and behold I am alive forevermore, and I have the keys of Death and Hades.” The same one who is glorious is the one who died. His keys mean that death and the grave answer to him. No one needs to fear them.

He tells John to write what he has seen, what is now, and what will take place after this. The seven stars and lampstands are explained: the stars are the angels (or messengers) of the churches, and the lampstands are the churches themselves. Jesus walks among his churches. He knows them, holds them, and judges them. Interpreters have understood Revelation in different ways: as largely about events in the first century (preterist), as the sweep of church history (historicist), as symbols of the spiritual struggle across all ages (idealist), or as largely about events at the end of history (futurist). Many thoughtful readers combine elements of these. In every approach, the center is clear: Christ is Lord, and his church is held in his hand.
connection: Daniel 7:9-14 and 10:5-6 stand behind the vision of the Son of Man. Exodus 19:5-6 is the source of “a kingdom, priests.” Zechariah 12:10 and Matthew 24:30 relate to verse 7. Isaiah 41:4 and 44:6 are behind the Alpha and Omega and the first and last. Ezekiel 1 and Isaiah 6 show similar overwhelming visions. John 1:1-18 and Philippians 2:9-11 speak of Christ’s glory. Hebrews 2:14-15 speaks of the defeat of death. Acts 4:12 and Romans 14:9 speak of Christ’s lordship. 1 Peter 2:9 says believers are a royal priesthood. Zechariah 4 describes the lampstand.
application:
Read the book aloud today, as the blessing in verse 3 invites. Even reading the first chapter aloud will help you hear it as its first audience did.

Picture the risen Christ walking among your church. What would he commend, and what would he correct?

When you fear death or what is ahead, say verse 18 to yourself: the living one holds the keys.
prayerPrompts: Worship Jesus, the faithful witness and ruler of kings.
Thank him for loving you and freeing you from your sins.
Ask him to keep you from fear, and listen to him say, “Fear not.”
